questions.question: Which change would increase the distance between adjacent maxima from a diffraction grating? A: decrease grating-screen distance; B: decrease distance between grating lines; C: decrease intensity; D: decrease wavelength.
questions.answer: B - decreasing the line spacing d increases the separation of maxima.
steps: At small angles the separation of maxima is x = lambda x D / d.
x depends on wavelength lambda, screen distance D and line spacing d.
A: decreasing D reduces x, so wrong.
B: decreasing d (lines closer together) increases x, so correct.
C: intensity does not change the position of maxima.
D: decreasing lambda reduces x, so wrong.

questions.question: Explain why treating electromagnetic radiation as a particle (photon) is more successful than a wave model for the photoelectric effect.
questions.answer: The photon model explains threshold frequency, instant emission and KE depending on frequency; the wave model does not.
steps: Wave model: energy spreads over the wavefront, so an electron would need time to absorb enough energy, giving a delay.
Wave model predicts electrons emitted at any frequency if intensity is high enough, with KE rising with intensity.
Photon model: each photon carries E = hf and is absorbed by one electron in a single interaction.
A threshold frequency f0 = phi/h exists; below it no emission whatever the intensity.
Max KE = hf - phi depends on frequency; intensity only changes the number of photons, so number of electrons.
Emission is observed to be instantaneous, which matches the photon model.

questions.question: Using the hydrogen energy level diagram, determine the transition that releases a photon of frequency 7.48e13 Hz.
questions.answer: Transition from -0.54 eV to -0.85 eV.
steps: Look for two levels 0.31 eV apart: -0.54 - (-0.85) = 0.31 eV.
A photon is released when the electron falls, so the transition is from -0.54 eV down to -0.85 eV.

questions.question: Calculate the minimum Earth-Sun distance given maximum intensity 1.41 kW m^-2 at Earth and Sun power 3.83e26 W.
steps: Intensity from a point source: I = P / (4 pi r^2), power spread over a sphere.
Minimum distance corresponds to maximum intensity, I = 1410 W m^-2.
r = sqrt(P / (4 pi I)) = sqrt(3.83e26 / (4 pi x 1410)).

questions.question: Mars receives radiation varying from 491 to 711 W m^-2. Explain two differences between the orbits of Mars and Earth deduced from this and Earth's data (1.32 to 1.41 kW m^-2).
questions.answer: Mars has a more elliptical orbit (distance ratio about 1.20 vs 1.03) and lies further from the Sun (closest approach about 2.07e11 m).
steps: Intensity is proportional to 1/r^2, so r_max/r_min = sqrt(I_max/I_min).
Difference 1: Mars has a larger variation in distance, so its orbit is more elliptical.
Difference 2: Mars's closest approach has intensity 711 vs Earth's 1410 W m^-2, giving r = 1.47e11 x sqrt(1410/711) = 2.07e11 m.
So Mars orbits further from the Sun than Earth.

questions.question: A solar panel has a surface area of 1.54 m^2. The intensity of radiation incident on the Earth's surface is 1050 W m^-2. The manufacturer states that the maximum output power of the solar panel is 250 W. Which could be used to calculate the maximum efficiency of the solar panel? A (250 x 1.54) / 1050; B 1050 / (250 x 1.54); C (1050 x 1.54) / 250; D 250 / (1050 x 1.54).
steps: Efficiency = useful power output / total power input.
Power input = intensity x area = 1050 x 1.54 W.
So efficiency = 250 / (1050 x 1.54), about 0.155. The other options invert the ratio or multiply the output by the area.

questions.question: Which has the largest de Broglie wavelength: A electron at 3.0e5 m/s; B electron at 4.0e5 m/s; C neutron at 3.0e5 m/s; D neutron at 4.0e5 m/s?
questions.answer: A - electron travelling at 3.0e5 m s-1.
steps: de Broglie wavelength lambda = h / (m v), so the largest wavelength has the smallest momentum mv.
Electron mass 9.11e-31 kg; neutron mass 1.67e-27 kg (about 1800 times larger).
A: electron momentum = 9.11e-31 x 3.0e5 = 2.73e-25 kg m s-1.
B, C and D all have larger momentum (B 3.64e-25; C about 5.0e-22; D about 6.7e-22 kg m s-1).
So A has the largest wavelength.

questions.question: Describe the process by which visible light (589 nm) is emitted from sodium atoms in a gas discharge tube.
questions.answer: Collisions excite atomic electrons to higher levels; when they fall back they emit photons whose energy equals the level difference.
steps: Fast electrons from the high p.d. collide with sodium atoms and transfer energy.
An atomic electron absorbs this energy and is excited to a higher energy level.
The excited electron is unstable and falls back to a lower level.
Each fall emits a photon with E = hf equal to the energy difference between the two levels.
Fixed level differences give a specific frequency, so a line of 589 nm is seen.

questions.question: Calculate the energy in eV of a photon of visible light with wavelength 589 nm.
steps: E = hf = hc / lambda: photon energy from wavelength.
1 eV = 1.60e-19 J, so convert the energy.

questions.question: A 300 lines/mm grating is used with lambda = 589 nm. Measured s = 0.234 m (central to first order) and D = 1.30 m. Determine whether the 300 lines/mm label is correct.
questions.answer: Yes, approximately: the measurements give about 301 lines/mm, consistent with 300 lines/mm.
steps: Diffraction grating equation: d sin(theta) = n lambda, with n = 1.
d = lambda / sin(theta) = 589e-9 / 0.177 = 3.32e-6 m.
Lines per mm = 1 / (3.32e-6 m) = 1 / (3.32e-3 mm) = 301 lines/mm.
Difference from 300 is about 0.3%, within measurement error, so the label is correct.

questions.question: Ultraviolet light is incident on a metal surface and photoelectrons are released. The number of photoelectrons released per second is N and the maximum kinetic energy of the released electrons is E_k. Which pair of graphs shows how N and E_k vary with the intensity I of the incident light? A N constant, E_k increases linearly with I; B N increases linearly with I (through the origin), E_k constant; C N and E_k both increase linearly with I; D N and E_k both constant.
questions.answer: B: N is proportional to I and E_k is constant.
steps: Higher intensity means more photons arriving per second. Each photon releases at most one electron, so N is proportional to I (a straight line through the origin).
The maximum kinetic energy E_k = hf - phi depends on the photon frequency and the work function only, not on the number of photons, so it stays constant as I changes.

questions.question: A student writes: "If every particle has a de Broglie wavelength, it should be possible for a moving car to have the same de Broglie wavelength as a fast moving electron, although the car would be moving very slowly." Determine whether the student's statement about the speed of the car is mathematically correct. Speed of electron = 1.5 x 10^7 m s^-1; mass of car = 900 kg.
questions.answer: The statement is correct: the car would need a speed of about 1.5 x 10^-26 m s^-1, which is extremely slow.
steps: De Broglie wavelength lambda = h / (m v), so equal wavelengths need equal momentum: m_car v_car = m_e v_e.
v_car = 1.5 x 10^-26 m s^-1, an extremely small speed (effectively stationary), so the student is right.

questions.question: Suggest why the de Broglie wavelength is not a useful property for a car.
questions.answer: A car's mass is very large, so its de Broglie wavelength is far too small to observe (about 5e-44 m for 900 kg at 1.5e7 m/s).
steps: de Broglie wavelength lambda = h / (m v).
A car's mass (900 kg) is enormous compared with an electron.
Example: lambda = 6.63e-34 / (900 x 1.5e7) = 4.9e-44 m.
Such a wavelength is far too small to show diffraction or be detected.

questions.question: State what is meant by work function.
questions.answer: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of a metal.
steps: Work function phi is the energy needed to free an electron from the metal surface.
The electron must escape the attraction of the metal's positive lattice.
A photon with hf >= phi can release a photoelectron.
It is quoted in eV or J and is specific to each metal.

questions.question: The work functions of four metals are: potassium 3.62 x 10^-19 J, magnesium 5.89 x 10^-19 J, tungsten 7.18 x 10^-19 J, iron 7.41 x 10^-19 J. When light with a frequency of 6.32 x 10^15 Hz is incident on a metal, photoelectrons are released with a maximum kinetic energy of 3.60 x 10^-18 J. Determine which of the four metals the light is incident on.
questions.answer: Magnesium.
steps: This matches the work function of magnesium (5.89 x 10^-19 J).

questions.question: UV intensity 38.0 mW m^-2 is absorbed over 8.10e-20 m^2 by a potassium atom. Calculate the time for the atom to absorb enough energy to release an electron.
questions.answer: Time taken = 1.2 x 10^2 s (about 118 s).
steps: The work function of potassium (from the table) is 3.62 x 10^-19 J.
Intensity = 38.0 mW m^-2 = 3.80 x 10^-2 W m^-2. Power absorbed by the atom = I x A = 3.80 x 10^-2 x 8.10 x 10^-20 = 3.08 x 10^-21 W.
The wave model predicts a delay of about two minutes, whereas emission is observed to be instant.

questions.question: Explain how instantaneous electron emission provides evidence for the particle nature of electromagnetic radiation.
questions.answer: Instant emission means energy arrives in discrete packets (photons), each absorbed by one electron, not spread out like a wave.
steps: A wave model predicts a time delay while energy builds up on each electron.
Electrons are observed to be emitted immediately when UV is incident.
This means each electron absorbs enough energy in one interaction.
That energy arrives as a single photon, which is evidence of the particle nature of light.

questions.question: The evidence for the wave nature of electrons came from: A diffraction; B polarisation; C reflection; D refraction.
questions.answer: A - diffraction.
steps: Electron diffraction through crystals (G P Thomson, Davisson and Germer) gave interference patterns.
Diffraction is a wave property, so it shows electrons behave as waves.
Polarisation only occurs for transverse waves and is not used as electron evidence.
Reflection and refraction occur for particles too, so they do not show wave nature.

questions.question: Explain, using Huygens' construction, how diffraction occurs as waves pass through a gap.
questions.answer: Each point of the wavefront in the gap acts as a source of secondary wavelets that spread into the region beyond the gap.
steps: Huygens: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets.
Points at the edges of the gap emit wavelets that spread around the edges into the shadow region.
When the gap is comparable to the wavelength, these wavelets spread significantly.
The new wavefront beyond the gap is curved, so the wave spreads out (diffraction).

questions.question: Sketch a graph of intensity against position along line AB across the circular diffraction pattern.
questions.answer: A symmetrical graph with a tall central maximum at the middle of AB and weaker outer maxima that decrease in height away from the centre, with zero intensity between them.
steps: The centre of AB is the position of greatest intensity: draw one tall peak there.
On each side the intensity falls to about zero (dark ring) and then rises to a much smaller secondary maximum.
Each further maximum is lower than the one before it, so the peak heights decrease outwards.
The graph is symmetrical about the centre, and the central peak is about twice as wide as the secondary peaks.

questions.question: Calculate the maximum energy received by solar panels covering the Sahara (area 9.2e12 m^2) in one hour, given maximum intensity 1100 W m^-2.
steps: Energy received in time t is E = P t, where P = I A.
Power received P = I x A = 1100 x 9.2e12 = 1.01e16 W.
Time t = 1 hour = 3600 s.

questions.question: Determine whether covering the Sahara with solar panels could generate enough electricity for the whole world (23 800 TWh per year, 1 TWh = 3.6e15 J).
questions.answer: Yes, in principle: the maximum yearly input (about 3.2e23 J) is roughly 3700 times world annual use (8.57e19 J).
steps: World annual use = 23 800 x 3.6e15 = 8.57e19 J.
Maximum energy in one hour (3.64e19 J) is already about 0.43 of this.
Over one year at maximum intensity (8760 h): 8760 x 3.64e19 = 3.19e23 J.
This is about 3700 times world annual use, so even allowing for night, angle and efficiency the margin is large.

questions.question: Explain why sand storms reduce the power generated by solar panels.
questions.answer: Sand settles on or scatters and absorbs sunlight, so less radiation reaches the cells and less power is produced.
steps: Sand particles settle on the panel surface.
They absorb or scatter incident sunlight, so less radiation reaches the solar cells.
Lower incident intensity means less power input to the cells.
Hence the electrical output power is reduced.

questions.question: Calculate the ionisation energy E in eV of a hydrogen atom using Bohr's expression with k = 8.85e-12 C V^-1 m^-1, m = electron mass, e = electron charge and h.
questions.answer: E = 13.5 eV (about 2.17e-18 J), i.e. about 13.6 eV.
steps: Bohr ionisation energy E = m e^4 / (8 k^2 h^2) (the formula image is not in the text; this is the standard form).
Use m = 9.11e-31 kg (electron mass, not given in text) and e = 1.60e-19 C.

questions.question: A student says neutrons moving at 1.4e7 m/s have a wavelength similar to the radius of a hydrogen atom. Determine whether the student is correct (neutron mass 1.67e-27 kg).
questions.answer: Incorrect: the neutron wavelength is about 2.8e-14 m, about 1900 times smaller than the atomic radius of about 5.3e-11 m.
steps: Bohr radius (n = 1): r = k h^2 / (pi m e^2) (standard form; formula image not in text).
Neutron de Broglie wavelength: lambda = h / (m v) = 6.63e-34 / (1.67e-27 x 1.4e7).
Ratio r / lambda = 5.31e-11 / 2.84e-14 = about 1900.
The wavelength is far smaller than the atom, so the student is incorrect.

questions.question: Which is an experimental observation of the photoelectric effect? A: electrons released only after long exposure; B: increasing frequency increases max KE; C: increasing intensity increases max KE; D: only wavelength above a threshold releases electrons.
questions.answer: B - increasing the frequency increases the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons.
steps: A is wrong: electrons are emitted almost instantly.
B is correct: KE max = hf - phi increases with frequency.
C is wrong: intensity does not change max KE, only the number of electrons.
D is wrong: emission needs frequency above a threshold, so wavelength must be below a threshold.

questions.question: Explain why immediate discharge of a zinc plate by UV cannot be explained by the wave model of electromagnetic radiation.
questions.answer: The wave model predicts a delay while energy builds up on electrons, but emission was immediate, which supports photons.
steps: Wave model: energy is spread over the wavefront, so electrons need time to absorb enough energy.
This predicts a delay before electrons are released, especially at low intensity.
The gold leaf began falling back immediately, so electrons were emitted instantly.
This matches a photon model in which one photon is absorbed by one electron.

questions.question: UV photons of energy 9.3e-19 J hit zinc (work function 4.3 eV). Calculate the maximum speed of released electrons.
steps: Work function in joules: 4.3 eV x 1.60e-19 = 6.88e-19 J.

questions.question: Discuss a student's suggestion that greater electron speed results from both a lower work function metal and UV of greater wavelength.
questions.answer: Not valid as stated: a lower work function raises KE max, but a longer wavelength lowers photon energy and reduces it.
steps: Max KE = hf - phi, so a lower work function increases KE max (first part correct).
A longer wavelength means lower frequency and lower photon energy E = hc/lambda.
This lowers KE max (second part incorrect).
The two changes oppose each other, so speed increases only if the work function fall exceeds the photon energy fall.

questions.question: A smart meter emits 1.00 W of radio waves. A person stands 25 cm away. Deduce whether the intensity is dangerous (above 4.5 W m^-2).
questions.answer: I = 1.27 W m^-2, which is below 4.5 W m^-2, so not dangerous.
steps: Intensity from a point source: I = P / (4 pi r^2).
This is below the dangerous limit of 4.5 W m^-2, so not dangerous (assuming uniform spreading).

questions.question: Calculate the energy in eV of a photon emitted by a smart meter at frequency 902 MHz.
steps: Photon energy E = hf.

questions.question: The display of the smart meter in one household shows the total electrical energy used in one day: 6.85 kWh. 1 kW h is a unit of energy equivalent to 1 kW of power used for 1 hour. The kettle in this house has a power of 1200 W. The kettle takes 125 seconds to heat the water to boiling, then switches off. A student suggests that boiling the kettle once uses less than 1% of the total energy shown on the smart meter display. Assess the student's suggestion.
questions.answer: The suggestion is correct: one boil uses about 0.61 % of the 6.85 kWh.
steps: Energy used by the kettle = P t = 1200 W x 125 s = 1.5 x 10^5 J (0.0417 kWh).
Total energy on the display = 6.85 kWh = 6.85 x 3.6 x 10^6 J = 2.47 x 10^7 J.
0.61 % is less than 1 %, so the student is correct.

questions.question: Explain the process that results in emission of a small number of different visible wavelengths from excited hydrogen, referring to energy levels.
questions.answer: Electrons are excited to higher discrete levels and drop back, emitting photons whose energies equal the level differences.
steps: Atoms absorb energy, so electrons move up to higher discrete energy levels.
Energy levels are fixed, so only specific energy differences are possible.
Excited electrons fall back to lower levels, possibly in several steps.
Each fall emits a photon with E = hf = energy difference between levels.
Different level pairs give different frequencies, so only some visible wavelengths are emitted.
This gives a line spectrum with discrete wavelengths.

questions.question: Explain why light emitted by excited atoms in air has a large number of different wavelengths.
questions.answer: Air contains many different gas atoms and molecules, each with many energy levels, so a large number of transitions occur.
steps: Air is a mixture of gases such as nitrogen and oxygen.
Each species has its own set of energy levels.
Many atoms are excited, so many different transitions can occur.
Each transition gives a photon of different energy, so many wavelengths are produced.

questions.question: A light bulb with an efficiency of 12% is positioned 2.0 m above a light sensor. The intensity of light at the light sensor is 0.14 W m^-2. Which could be used to calculate the power of the light bulb? A (0.14) x (0.12) x (4 pi) x (2.0)^2; B (0.14) x (4 pi) x (2.0)^2 / 0.12; C (0.14) x (0.12) x (pi) x (2.0)^2; D (0.14) x (pi) x (2.0)^2 / 0.12.
steps: The light spreads out over a sphere of radius 2.0 m, so the light power emitted P_light = I x 4 pi r^2 = 0.14 x 4 pi x 2.0^2 = 7.0 W.
Only 12 % of the electrical power is emitted as light, so P_bulb = P_light / 0.12.

questions.question: UV of wavelength 20.0 nm is incident on a metal of work function 3.68 eV. Calculate the maximum speed of the emitted electrons.
steps: Photon energy E = hc / lambda = (6.63e-34 x 3.00e8) / 20.0e-9 = 9.95e-18 J.
Work function = 3.68 x 1.60e-19 = 5.89e-19 J.

questions.topic: Intensity And Wavelength Effect On KE
questions.question: A student suggests increasing both wavelength and intensity increases the maximum speed of photoelectrons. Explain whether this is correct.
questions.answer: Incorrect: max KE depends on photon frequency; a longer wavelength lowers it, and intensity does not change it.
steps: Max KE = hf - phi depends on the energy of each photon, not on intensity.
Increasing intensity only increases the number of photons, so more electrons, not faster ones.
Increasing wavelength lowers the frequency and so the photon energy.
Lower photon energy means lower max KE, so the combined suggestion is incorrect.

questions.question: Which wavefront diagram (A to D, gaps of different sizes) shows diffracted wavefronts that are not semicircular?
questions.answer: B: the gap is much wider than the wavelength, so the diffracted wavefronts are not semicircular.
steps: Diffracted wavefronts are semicircular only when the gap is about the size of the wavelength or smaller.
In A the gap is about equal to the wavelength, and in C it is narrower than the wavelength, so both spread out in semicircles. In D the gap is only about 1.5 wavelengths.
In B the wavefronts are close together (short wavelength) and the gap is about four wavelengths wide, so most of the wavefront passes straight through with only slight bending at the edges.

questions.question: An electron drops from -0.54 eV to -13.60 eV, releasing at least one photon. Which energy could NOT be produced? A: 0.31 eV; B: 0.54 eV; C: 12.09 eV; D: 13.06 eV.
questions.answer: B - 0.54 eV, since no pair of hydrogen levels differs by 0.54 eV.
steps: Direct transition -0.54 to -13.60 eV emits 13.06 eV (D possible).
Cascade via -0.85 eV gives 0.31 eV (A possible) and then 12.75 eV; via -1.51 eV gives 0.97 eV then 12.09 eV (C possible).
A single photon of 0.54 eV would need levels separated by 0.54 eV, and no such pair exists in hydrogen.
Hydrogen levels are -13.6/n^2 eV, and no pair differs by 0.54 eV, so B is impossible.

questions.question: Calculate the intensity of solar radiation at ICESat-2, distance 1.50e11 m from the Sun, with Sun power 3.83e26 W.
steps: Intensity from a point source spreads over a sphere: I = P / (4 pi r^2).
Substitute r = 1.50e11 m: r^2 = 2.25e22 m^2.

questions.question: The laser emits light of wavelength 532 nm. Calculate the energy in joules of each photon.
steps: Photon energy E = hf = hc / lambda.
lambda = 532e-9 m.

questions.question: Photons travel to Earth and back in a mean time of 3.20 ms. Calculate the height ICESat-2 orbits above Earth.
steps: Light travels at c = 3.00e8 m s-1 for the round trip.
Total distance = c t = 3.00e8 x 3.20e-3 = 9.60e5 m.
The distance covers up and back, so height = total / 2.
Height = 4.80e5 m (480 km).

questions.question: Suggest why only photons of exactly 532 nm are used in analysing the returned photons.
questions.answer: Filtering keeps only laser photons, removing background light and improving the signal-to-noise ratio.
steps: Background sunlight contains a wide range of wavelengths.
The laser emits one wavelength (532 nm) only.
Filtering to 532 nm removes most of the background signal.
This improves the signal-to-noise ratio of the detected photons.

questions.question: Explain how ICESat-2 measurements show that an ice sheet 1000 m above sea level has a flat surface and is higher than sea level.
questions.answer: Equal return times across the sheet show it is flat; shorter return times than sea level show it is higher.
steps: Round trip time gives the distance from the satellite to the surface.
If the return time is the same at every point along the sheet, the surface is flat.
Sea level is 1000 m further, so the extra round trip time is 2 x 1000 / 3.00e8 = 6.7e-6 s.
The ice returns the pulse sooner than sea level would, so the ice is higher than sea level.

questions.question: Explain why a 12.3 eV electron excites hydrogen from -13.6 eV to -1.5 eV, but a 12.3 eV photon is not absorbed.
questions.answer: A collision can transfer the required 12.1 eV from a 12.3 eV electron, but a photon must match the 12.1 eV difference exactly.
steps: Energy needed for the transition -13.6 to -1.5 eV is 12.1 eV.
An electron collision can transfer any amount up to its KE (12.3 eV), keeping the remaining 0.2 eV.
A photon is absorbed only if its energy exactly equals a level difference.
A 12.3 eV photon does not match 12.1 eV, so it is not absorbed and the electron stays at -13.6 eV.

questions.question: Which demonstrates the photon model of light? A: diffraction patterns; B: Huygens' construction; C: photoelectric effect; D: plane polarisation.
questions.answer: C - the photoelectric effect.
steps: Photon model: light energy comes in packets E = hf.
Photoelectric effect: one photon ejects one electron above threshold frequency.
Diffraction, Huygens construction and plane polarisation are wave evidence.
So C is the only demonstration of the photon model.

questions.question: Which statement about the de Broglie equation is correct? A: wavelength independent of mass; B: can calculate photon momentum; C: p is electron mass times c; D: h depends on particle.
questions.answer: B - the de Broglie equation rearranges to p = h / lambda, which also gives a photon's momentum.
steps: de Broglie equation: lambda = h / p, so p = h / lambda.
This applies to photons too, giving photon momentum p = h / lambda.
A is wrong: lambda depends on mass through p = mv.
C is wrong: p is momentum mv. D is wrong: h is a universal constant.

questions.question: A moving electron has a de Broglie wavelength of 656 nm. Which could be used to determine the speed of the electron? A 6.63 x 10^-34 / ((656 x 10^-9)(9.11 x 10^-31)); B (656 x 10^-9)(9.11 x 10^-31) / 6.63 x 10^-34; C (656 x 10^-9)(6.63 x 10^-34) / 9.11 x 10^-31; D 9.11 x 10^-31 / ((656 x 10^-9)(6.63 x 10^-34)).
steps: de Broglie: lambda = h / (m v), so v = h / (m lambda).
Substituting h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s, m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg and lambda = 656 x 10^-9 m gives option A (about 1.1 x 10^3 m s^-1).

questions.question: Explain how the apparatus (signal generator, speaker, microphone, oscilloscope) can determine the speed of sound in air.
questions.answer: Measure the distance moved between repeated in-phase positions to find lambda, then use v = f x lambda.
steps: The signal generator sets the frequency f of the sound from the speaker.
The oscilloscope shows the phase relationship between the source trace and the microphone trace.
Move the microphone along the line from the speaker until the traces are in phase again.
The distance d moved over n complete cycles gives lambda = d / n.
Speed v = f x lambda; the time scale on the oscilloscope can also give the period T = 1/f.

questions.question: Explain what change the student made to the microphone position between Photograph 2 and Photograph 3.
questions.answer: The microphone was moved along the line by a whole number of wavelengths (for example one wavelength) towards or away from the loudspeaker, since the traces are in antiphase again.
steps: In Photograph 2 the peaks of one trace are directly above the troughs of the other: the traces are in antiphase (phase difference 180 deg).
In Photograph 3 the traces are again in antiphase (each peak is over a trough of the other trace), so the phase difference is unchanged.
The phase difference only repeats when the path from loudspeaker to microphone changes by a whole number of wavelengths (moving by half a wavelength would turn antiphase into in phase).
So the microphone was moved a distance of one wavelength (or n wavelengths) along the line, which is how the wavelength can be measured.

questions.question: Show that radiation of wavelength 280 nm has a photon energy of about 4.4 eV.
questions.answer: E = 7.10e-19 J = 4.4 eV (shown).
steps: Photon energy E = hc / lambda.
lambda = 280 nm = 2.80e-7 m.
Convert: 7.10e-19 / 1.60e-19 = 4.44 eV, about 4.4 eV.

questions.question: Explain the conclusions that can be drawn from the student's statements about photoelectric emission from copper and zinc with sources A (2.0 eV) and B (4.4 eV).
questions.answer: Photon energy must exceed the work function for electrons to be released, so there is a threshold: 2.0 eV is below both work functions; 4.4 eV is above the work function of zinc but below that of copper; intensity changes the rate of emission, not whether emission occurs. This supports the photon (particle) model of light.
steps: Source A (2.0 eV): no electrons from either metal, however intense, so 2.0 eV is less than the work function of both copper and zinc. A photon gives all its energy to one electron, so raising the intensity (more photons) cannot help.
Source B (4.4 eV) releases electrons from zinc but not copper: so phi(zinc) is less than 4.4 eV and phi(copper) is greater than 4.4 eV. Different metals have different work functions.
Putting these together: 2.0 eV < phi(zinc) < 4.4 eV < phi(copper) (zinc is 4.30 eV).
Increasing the intensity of B on zinc means more photons per second, so more electrons per second are released (rate proportional to intensity).

Conclusion: emission depends on photon energy (frequency) exceeding the work function, not on intensity. This cannot be explained by the wave model, where energy would build up, but fits light as photons with energy hf.

questions.question: Which of four electron transitions (A to D) emits a photon with the longest wavelength?
questions.answer: A.
steps: A photon is emitted only when an electron drops to a lower level, so only the downward arrows A and B are emissions (C and D are upward: absorption).
Photon energy = hc / lambda, so the longest wavelength comes from the smallest energy gap.
A is the smaller drop (top level to the middle level), while B is a larger drop to the ground state, so A has the least energy and the longest wavelength.

questions.question: Explain how the pattern produced when electrons pass through a thin metal foil is evidence for wave rather than particle behaviour.
questions.answer: The pattern is a set of concentric bright and dark rings, which is a diffraction pattern; diffraction and interference occur only for waves, so the electrons are behaving as waves.
steps: The screen shows concentric rings of alternating bright and dark regions, a diffraction pattern.

The electrons are diffracted by the regularly spaced atoms in the foil (spacing similar to their de Broglie wavelength), and the diffracted waves interfere: constructively at the bright rings, destructively at the dark rings.

Particles would pass straight through, or scatter randomly, giving a central spot or a diffuse patch rather than a pattern of maxima and minima. Diffraction and interference are wave properties, so this is evidence of wave behaviour.

questions.question: A grating of 450 lines/mm produces the next bright dot at X. Determine the laser wavelength from the diagram.
questions.answer: Wavelength = 6.3 x 10^-7 m (630 nm).
steps: Line spacing d = 1 / (450 x 10^3 lines per m) = 2.22 x 10^-6 m.
X is the first order maximum (n = 1): tan theta = 0.500 / 1.690, so theta = 16.5 deg.
lambda = d sin theta / n = 2.22 x 10^-6 x sin 16.5 deg = 2.22 x 10^-6 x 0.2837.
lambda = 6.30 x 10^-7 m = 630 nm.

questions.question: Explain why a series of bright dots is seen on the screen when the laser is switched on.
questions.answer: Light from many slits interferes; constructive interference occurs at angles where d sin(theta) = n lambda, forming bright maxima.
steps: The grating has many equally spaced slits, each diffracting the laser light.
Light from all slits interferes at the screen.
Constructive interference (maxima) occurs where d sin(theta) = n lambda.
Destructive interference between maxima gives dark regions, so separate bright dots appear.

questions.question: Suggest what would be observed on the screen if the laser is replaced by a parallel beam of white light.
questions.answer: A white central maximum, with coloured spectra on either side (violet nearest the centre, red furthest).
steps: Each wavelength has maxima at a different angle, since d sin(theta) = n lambda.
The central maximum is white, as all wavelengths are at zero angle.
On either side, the colours separate into spectra, with violet closest to the centre.
Higher orders overlap, so the dots become coloured spectra.

questions.question: State what is meant by work function.
questions.answer: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of a metal.
steps: Work function phi is the minimum energy needed to free an electron from the surface.
Photons must have energy hf >= phi to release electrons.
Work function is a property of the metal, measured in eV or J.
At threshold the emitted electron has zero kinetic energy.

questions.question: Ultraviolet light is incident on a zinc plate. The UV section is split into UVC (200-280 nm), UVB (280-320 nm) and UVA (320-400 nm). The minimum de Broglie wavelength of the released electrons is 1.50 x 10^-9 m. Deduce whether the ultraviolet light incident on the zinc plate is UVA, UVB or UVC. Work function of zinc = 4.30 eV.
questions.answer: UVC (the wavelength is about 250 nm).
steps: The shortest de Broglie wavelength belongs to the electrons with the greatest momentum, i.e. the maximum kinetic energy.
Photon energy = phi + E_k(max) = 4.30 + 0.67 = 4.97 eV = 7.95 x 10^-19 J.
250 nm lies in the range 200-280 nm, so the light is UVC.

questions.question: A student used a zinc plate and UV light of different frequencies. The graph of maximum kinetic energy (eV) against frequency (x 10^14 Hz) is a straight line through (7.5, 0), (9.0, 2), (10.5, 4), (12.0, 6), (13.5, 8) and (15.0, 10). Einstein's photoelectric equation hf = phi + (1/2)mv^2 applies. Describe two ways that the graph is not consistent with the values known for a zinc plate. Your answer should include calculations. Work function of zinc = 4.30 eV.
questions.answer: (1) The threshold frequency is 7.5 x 10^14 Hz on the graph (phi = 3.1 eV) but should be 1.04 x 10^15 Hz for phi = 4.30 eV. (2) The gradient is 1.33 x 10^-14 eV s (2.1 x 10^-33 J s), more than three times the Planck constant (4.14 x 10^-15 eV s).
steps: The gradient of a graph of E_k against f should equal h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s = 4.14 x 10^-15 eV s, i.e. 0.414 eV per 10^14 Hz.
The graph's gradient is 10 eV / (15.0 - 7.5) x 10^14 Hz = 1.33 x 10^-14 eV s = 2.1 x 10^-33 J s, about 3.2 times too big.
The intercept on the frequency axis is the threshold frequency f0 = phi / h. With phi = 4.30 eV it should be 4.30 / 4.14 x 10^-15 = 1.04 x 10^15 Hz (10.4 x 10^14 Hz).
The graph has f0 = 7.5 x 10^14 Hz, which corresponds to phi = h f0 = 4.14 x 10^-15 x 7.5 x 10^14 = 3.1 eV, not 4.30 eV. (Also, at 15.0 x 10^14 Hz E_k should be 6.2 - 4.3 = 1.9 eV, not 10 eV.)

questions.question: Explain how photoelectric effect observations demonstrate that light behaves as a particle.
questions.answer: Instant emission, a threshold frequency, and KE depending only on frequency show light arrives as photons.
steps: Emission is instantaneous, even at low intensity, so energy is not built up over time.
Emission occurs only above a threshold frequency, whatever the intensity.
Max KE = hf - phi depends on frequency, not intensity.
Each electron absorbs one photon of energy hf in a single interaction.
Intensity only changes the number of photons, hence the number of electrons.
A wave model cannot explain these results, so light behaves as photons.

questions.question: In 1927 electrons passing through a nickel crystal produced a diffraction pattern. What can be concluded? A: particles; B: waves; C: both; D: neither.
questions.answer: B - electrons behave as waves.
steps: A diffraction pattern is a wave property.
Electrons were diffracted by the nickel crystal lattice, giving a pattern.
So electrons must behave as waves.
The observation gives no evidence of particle-only behaviour, so A, C and D are not concluded.

questions.question: Deduce the colour of visible light absorbed when an electron is excited from -3.40 eV to -1.50 eV in hydrogen (colour wavelength table missing).
questions.answer: Red light (wavelength about 654 nm).
steps: The photon energy equals the energy gap, so lambda = hc / E = 6.63 x 10^-34 x 3.00 x 10^8 / 3.04 x 10^-19.
lambda = 6.54 x 10^-7 m = 654 nm.
654 nm lies in the range 620-750 nm, so the light is red.

questions.question: Sirius A is 8.60 light years away and its intensity at Earth is 1.17e-7 W m^-2. Calculate its power.
questions.answer: About 9.7e27 W
steps: One light year = c x 1 year = 3.00e8 x 3.156e7 = 9.47e15 m.
Distance d = 8.60 x 9.47e15 = 8.14e16 m.
Power P = I x 4 pi d^2 = 1.17e-7 x 4 pi x (8.14e16)^2.

questions.question: Explain why only certain wavelengths of light are emitted when hydrogen gas is excited in the laboratory.
questions.answer: Electrons occupy discrete energy levels, so only photons with fixed energy differences are emitted.
steps: Electrons in an atom can only occupy discrete energy levels.
Transitions between levels have fixed energy differences.
Each transition emits a photon with E = hf equal to that difference.
So only certain frequencies and wavelengths appear in the line spectrum.

questions.question: When the distance between the Sun and the planet Mercury is 4.60 x 10^10 m, the intensity of solar radiation at the surface of Mercury is 1.45 x 10^4 W m^-2. Which expression gives the power of the Sun? A (1.45 x 10^4)(pi)(4.60 x 10^10)^2; B (1.45 x 10^4)(4 pi)(4.60 x 10^10)^2; C (1.45 x 10^4) / ((pi)(4.60 x 10^10)^2); D (1.45 x 10^4) / ((4 pi)(4.60 x 10^10)^2).
steps: Intensity = power / area, so P = I x A.
The Sun radiates equally in all directions, so at distance r the power is spread over a sphere of area 4 pi r^2.

questions.question: Which could NOT have caused the electron transition shown in the hydrogen diagram (A: absorb 13.6 eV photon; B: absorb 10.2 eV photon; C: 13.6 eV electron collision; D: 10.2 eV electron collision)?
questions.answer: A: the atom absorbing a photon with an energy of 13.6 eV.
steps: The transition is from -13.6 eV to -3.4 eV, which needs 13.6 - 3.4 = 10.2 eV.
An atom can only absorb a photon whose energy exactly matches an energy gap, so a 10.2 eV photon (B) can do it, but a 13.6 eV photon (A) does not match this gap and cannot cause it.
An electron colliding with the atom can transfer part of its kinetic energy, so electrons of 10.2 eV (D) or 13.6 eV (C) could both excite the atom (the 13.6 eV electron keeps the extra 3.4 eV).
lambda = h / (m v), so v = h / (m lambda).
The mass needed is the electron mass 9.11 x 10^-31 kg (not the charge 1.60 x 10^-19 C), which gives option A.

questions.topic: Max KE Less Than Photon Energy
questions.question: Explain why the maximum KE of a released electron is less than the energy of each incident photon.
questions.answer: Part of each photon's energy is used to overcome the work function, so KE max = hf - phi is less than hf.
steps: Each photon transfers its energy hf to one electron.
The electron must use energy phi (the work function) to escape the surface.
The remaining energy becomes kinetic energy: KE max = hf - phi.
Since phi is greater than zero, KE max is less than hf.

questions.question: The frequencies of three sources of light are: A 1.11 x 10^15 Hz, B 1.23 x 10^15 Hz, C 1.34 x 10^15 Hz. Light from one of the sources was incident on a magnesium plate and electrons were released with a maximum speed of 5.70 x 10^5 m s^-1. Deduce which of the three sources was used. Work function of magnesium = 3.68 eV.
questions.answer: Source A.
steps: This matches source A.

questions.question: Explain why the sound became quieter until no sound was heard as the student walked away from point X, referring to interference.
questions.answer: The path difference from the gaps grows to half a wavelength, causing destructive interference and zero sound.
steps: Sound from each gap spreads out and the two sets of waves are coherent.
At X the path difference is zero or a whole number of wavelengths, giving constructive interference and a loud sound.
As the student walks, the path difference from the two gaps increases.
At a path difference of half a wavelength, the waves arrive out of phase.
Destructive interference means the amplitudes cancel, so the sound becomes quieter.
At path difference lambda/2 the cancellation is complete and no sound is heard.

questions.question: Explain why two filament lamps on the same supply cannot produce a consistent interference pattern on a screen.
questions.answer: Filament lamps are not coherent: their random phases change rapidly, so no stable interference pattern forms.
steps: Interference needs two coherent sources with a constant phase difference.
Each filament emits light randomly from many atoms, so the phase changes continuously.
The phase difference between the two lamps is therefore not constant.
So the interference pattern is not stable on the screen.

questions.question: A solar panel 1.20 m x 0.80 m, intensity 1040 W m^-2, must supply at least 140 W to a pump. Calculate the minimum efficiency.
steps: Input power = I x A = 1040 x 0.960 = 998 W.
Efficiency = output power / input power = 140 / 998.
Efficiency = 0.140, i.e. 14.0%.

questions.question: Suggest two reasons why the efficiency calculated in (i) is the minimum that will operate the pump.
questions.answer: Real losses (wiring, pump) need more power, and lower real sunlight intensity would require higher efficiency.
steps: The pump needs at least 140 W, but wiring and pump losses mean more power is needed from the panel.
The calculation uses the maximum intensity of 1040 W m^-2 over the whole area.
Cloud, sun angle or dust reduce the incident intensity, so a higher efficiency would be needed.
Reflection and temperature losses also reduce real panel efficiency.

questions.question: Explain the difference between unpolarised light and plane polarised light.
questions.answer: Unpolarised light has E oscillating in all directions perpendicular to travel; plane polarised light has E in a single plane.
steps: Light is a transverse wave; the electric field oscillates perpendicular to travel.
In unpolarised light the oscillations occur in all planes/directions at random.
In plane polarised light the oscillations are confined to one fixed plane.
So unpolarised light has no preferred plane, while plane polarised light does.

questions.question: Describe how a student can demonstrate that sunlight is unpolarised.
questions.answer: Rotate a polariser in the sunlight: the transmitted intensity stays constant for unpolarised light.
steps: Place a polarising filter (polariser) in the path of the sunlight.
Rotate the filter through 360 degrees and observe the transmitted intensity.
For unpolarised light the intensity stays constant and does not drop to zero.
Plane polarised light would show maxima and zero transmission as the filter turns.

questions.question: A particle of speed 9.89e5 m/s has de Broglie wavelength 7.37e-10 m. Deduce whether its mass equals the electron mass.
questions.answer: Yes: m = 9.10e-31 kg, equal to the electron mass 9.11e-31 kg within rounding.
steps: de Broglie: lambda = h / (m v), so m = h / (lambda v).
This matches the electron mass (9.11e-31 kg) within rounding, so yes.

questions.question: The diagram shows some of the energy levels for a hydrogen atom: 0, -1.36 x 10^-19 J, -2.42 x 10^-19 J and -5.42 x 10^-19 J. Which expression is equal to the lowest frequency of light possible from a transition between these energy levels? A 5.42 x 10^-19 / 6.63 x 10^-34; B 1.36 x 10^-19 / 6.63 x 10^-34; C (2.42 x 10^-19 + 1.36 x 10^-19) / 6.63 x 10^-34; D (2.42 x 10^-19 - 1.36 x 10^-19) / 6.63 x 10^-34.
steps: f = Delta E / h, so the lowest frequency comes from the smallest energy gap.
The gaps (in 10^-19 J) are: 0 to -1.36 = 1.36; -1.36 to -2.42 = 1.06; -2.42 to -5.42 = 3.00 (larger gaps are bigger still).
The smallest gap is between -1.36 and -2.42: 2.42 - 1.36 = 1.06 x 10^-19 J, giving f = 1.6 x 10^14 Hz. This is option D.

questions.question: Photoelectrons leave a plate with maximum speed 3.51e5 m/s. Calculate their energy in eV.
steps: KE = (1/2) m v^2 with m = 9.11e-31 kg and v = 3.51e5 m s-1.

questions.question: The table shows work functions (x 10^-19 J): magnesium 5.89, aluminium 6.53, zinc 6.88, iron 7.20. The ultraviolet light used had a wavelength of 310 nm and released electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 0.351 eV. Deduce which of the metals was most likely to have been used as the metal plate.
questions.answer: Magnesium.
steps: This matches magnesium (5.89 x 10^-19 J). The other metals all have work functions above the photon energy of 6.42 x 10^-19 J, so they would not emit at all.

questions.question: Explain why photoelectrons are emitted only if the frequency of the incident radiation is above a particular value.
questions.answer: A single photon must supply at least the work function, so hf must be at least phi (threshold frequency).
steps: Each photon transfers its whole energy hf to a single electron.
The electron must gain at least the work function phi to escape the metal.
So hf must be greater than or equal to phi, giving a threshold frequency f0 = phi/h.
Below f0 no single photon has enough energy, however many photons (intensity) there are.

questions.question: Criticise the student's statement that photoelectrons can always be released if the light intensity is high enough, regardless of work function.
questions.answer: Wrong: intensity does not raise photon energy; the frequency must exceed the threshold set by the work function.
steps: Intensity changes only the number of photons per second, not the energy of each photon.
Each photon transfers hf to one electron.
If hf is less than the work function, no electron is released however intense the light.
So the statement is wrong: frequency must exceed the threshold for the metal.

questions.question: Explain why some wavelengths of white light are missing from the final reflected beam from the solar cell coating.
questions.answer: Waves reflected from the top and bottom surfaces interfere destructively for some wavelengths, so those are cancelled.
steps: White light contains a range of wavelengths.
Light reflected from the top and bottom coating surfaces travels different path lengths.
For some wavelengths the two reflected waves arrive out of phase (path difference and phase change).
These wavelengths interfere destructively and are cancelled from the reflected beam.

questions.question: White light is incident normally on a coating of refractive index 2.3 and thickness 6.5e-8 m. Calculate the visible wavelength missing from the reflected beam.
steps: Path difference in the coating at normal incidence is 2nd, with one reflection (top) giving a phase change of half a wavelength.
Destructive interference occurs when 2nd = (m + 1/2) lambda, for m = 0, 1, 2 ...
For m = 0: lambda = 2.99e-7 / 0.5 = 5.98e-7 m = 598 nm (visible); for m = 1 the wavelength is 199 nm (UV).

questions.question: A 8.7 m^2 solar array on a roof sloping at 60 degrees to horizontal receives 1.1 kW m^-2 perpendicular to the Sun's rays and outputs 5.4e6 J per hour. Calculate its efficiency.
questions.answer: About 31% (efficiency 0.31)
steps: Effective intensity on the roof = I cos(60) = 1100 x 0.5 = 550 W m^-2 (Sun's rays perpendicular to the ground).
Power input = 550 x 8.7 = 4785 W.
Energy input per hour = 4785 x 3600 = 1.72e7 J.

questions.question: A photon interacts with an electron in the -13.6 eV ground state of hydrogen. Explain why this causes emission of another photon.
questions.answer: The electron absorbs a photon to reach an excited level, then falls back and emits a photon of the level difference.
steps: The incident photon must have energy equal to a level difference to be absorbed.
Absorption raises the electron to an excited (unstable) energy level.
The electron falls back to a lower level.
The fall emits a photon with energy equal to the level difference.

questions.question: A photon has wavelength 218 nm. Determine its energy in eV.
steps: E = hc / lambda with lambda = 218e-9 m.
Use 1 eV = 1.60e-19 J.

questions.question: Explain whether the hydrogen atom could emit a photon of energy 5.70 eV.
questions.answer: No: 5.70 eV is not the difference between any two hydrogen energy levels.
steps: An atom emits a photon only when an electron falls between two allowed levels.
Hydrogen levels (standard values): -13.6, -3.40, -1.51, -0.85, -0.54 eV.
None equals 5.70 eV, so no single transition can emit this photon.

questions.question: Photons of energy 1.63e-18 J hit a metal with work function 5.89e-19 J. Calculate the maximum possible speed of the released electrons.
steps: KE = (1/2) m v^2, so v = sqrt(2 KE / m).

questions.question: Explain why the photoelectric effect demonstrates light behaving as a particle rather than a wave.
questions.answer: Instant emission, a threshold frequency and KE depending on frequency (not intensity) show light arrives as photons.
steps: Electrons are emitted immediately, with no delay as a wave would need to build up energy.
Emission needs a threshold frequency; intensity alone cannot release electrons.
Each photon transfers its whole energy hf to one electron.
Max KE depends on frequency only, which a wave model could not explain.

questions.question: Electrons are excited from the ground state to n = 3. How many different frequencies can be emitted as they return to the ground state? A: 1; B: 2; C: 3; D: 4.
questions.answer: C - 3 frequencies.
steps: Electrons from the ground state are excited to n = 3.
They can fall 3 to 1 directly, or cascade 3 to 2 and then 2 to 1.
Transitions possible: 3 to 1, 3 to 2 and 2 to 1.
Each has a different energy, so 3 different frequencies are emitted: answer C.
lambda = h / (m v), so v = h / (m lambda).

questions.question: Waves spread out as they pass an object. What is this process called? A: diffraction; B: interference; C: reflection; D: refraction.
questions.answer: A - diffraction.
steps: Waves spreading out as they pass an edge or obstacle is diffraction.
Interference is the combining of two or more waves.
Reflection is bouncing off a surface; refraction is change in direction on entering a new medium.
So A is the correct process.

questions.question: Earth and Jupiter orbit the Sun. The distance from Earth to the Sun is 1.49 x 10^11 m. The distance from Jupiter to the Sun is 7.78 x 10^11 m. The intensity of sunlight at Jupiter is I_J. Which can be used to calculate the intensity of the sunlight at Earth? A I_J x (7.78 x 10^11)^2 / (1.49 x 10^11)^2; B I_J x 4 pi x (7.78 x 10^11)^2 / (1.49 x 10^11)^2; C I_J x 7.78 x 10^11 / 1.49 x 10^11; D I_J x 4 pi x 7.78 x 10^11 / 1.49 x 10^11.
steps: Intensity = P / (4 pi r^2), so intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the Sun.
I_E / I_J = (r_J / r_E)^2, so I_E = I_J x (7.78 x 10^11 / 1.49 x 10^11)^2 (about 27 times I_J). The factor 4 pi cancels, so B and D are wrong; the square is needed, so C is wrong.

questions.question: Which does NOT occur when a light ray is incident on a glass block? A: diffraction; B: polarisation; C: reflection; D: refraction.
questions.answer: A - diffraction.
steps: Reflection and refraction occur at the glass surfaces.
Partial polarisation can occur at reflection from the glass surface.
Diffraction needs an aperture or edge, which the flat glass block does not provide.
So diffraction does not occur.

questions.question: A photon from a discharge tube has energy 3.44e-19 J. Calculate its frequency.
steps: Photon energy E = hf, so f = E / h.
Use h = 6.63e-34 J s.

questions.question: Explain how the large p.d. across a discharge tube causes the gas atoms to emit photons.
questions.answer: Electrons accelerated by the p.d. collide with gas atoms, exciting them; as electrons fall back, photons are emitted.
steps: The p.d. accelerates free electrons, which gain kinetic energy eV.
Electrons collide with gas atoms and transfer energy to them.
Atomic electrons are excited to higher discrete energy levels.
Excited electrons fall back to lower levels.
Each fall emits a photon with E = hf equal to the level difference.
Discrete level differences give a line spectrum of specific frequencies.

questions.question: Photons of 4.75 eV hit a metal with work function 6.30e-19 J. Show that the maximum electron speed is about 5.3e5 m/s.
questions.answer: v = 5.34e5 m s-1, about 5.3e5 m s-1 (shown).
steps: Photon energy = 4.75 x 1.60e-19 = 7.60e-19 J.
v = 5.34e5 m s-1, i.e. about 5.3e5 m s-1.

questions.question: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of electrons moving at 5.3e5 m/s.
steps: de Broglie wavelength lambda = h / (m v).
Use m = 9.11e-31 kg and v = 5.3e5 m s-1.

questions.question: A pulse-echo transducer detects an echo from a fish after 37 ms; sound speed in water is 1500 m/s. Calculate the distance to the fish.
steps: Sound travels to the fish and back, so total distance = v t.
Total distance = 1500 x 0.037 = 55.5 m.
Distance to the fish is half the total distance.
Distance = 55.5 / 2 = 27.8 m.

questions.question: Explain how the fixed time T between pulses affects the maximum distance at which a fish can be detected.
questions.answer: Maximum distance d = vT/2, so a longer T lets echoes from more distant fish return before the next pulse.
steps: An echo must return before the next pulse is emitted to be identified with that pulse.
Round trip time for a fish at distance d is 2d / v, which must not exceed T.
So maximum distance d_max = vT / 2.
A longer T allows a greater maximum distance.

questions.question: Explain how the frequency of the pulses should be adjusted to improve the accuracy of locating a fish.
questions.answer: Increase the frequency: a shorter wavelength gives better resolution of the fish's position.
steps: Wavelength lambda = v / f, so a higher frequency gives a shorter wavelength.
A shorter wavelength gives better resolution of small features.
Better resolution means the fish's position can be located more accurately.
So the frequency should be increased.

questions.question: Explain what the rings produced when an electron beam passes through graphite and hits a fluorescent screen show about the nature of electrons.
questions.answer: The rings are a diffraction pattern, showing that electrons have wave properties.
steps: Graphite has a regular crystal lattice with spacing of atomic order.
Electron waves diffract at the lattice planes, producing concentric rings.
A diffraction pattern is a wave property.
So electrons have wave properties (de Broglie).

questions.question: Layer 1 of a solar cell has work function 1.86 eV. Calculate the minimum frequency of light needed to release an electron from layer 1.
steps: Minimum photon energy equals the work function: phi = 1.86 x 1.60e-19 = 2.98e-19 J.
At threshold hf = phi.

questions.question: Layer 1 (higher work function) is removed so all photons reach layer 2. Explain how this affects the rate at which electrons are released, assuming each layer absorbs all photons above its threshold frequency.
questions.answer: The rate is unchanged: layer 2 absorbs all photons above its threshold, so the same total number of electrons is released per second.
steps: Layer 1 absorbs all photons with f above f1, releasing electrons in layer 1.
Layer 2 only receives photons not absorbed by layer 1, so it absorbs f2 < f < f1.
With layer 1 removed, layer 2 receives and absorbs all photons with f above f2.
Photons above f1 are no longer absorbed in layer 1 but are absorbed in layer 2 instead.
Total photons absorbed per second is the same in both cases, so the total rate of emission is unchanged.
The electrons now come from layer 2 with greater kinetic energy.

questions.question: Two cells (each emf 5.0 V, internal resistance 0.80 ohm) drive a 4.0 ohm resistor, giving 13 W in series. Deduce whether parallel connection gives less than half this power.
questions.answer: Correct: parallel gives about 5.2 W, which is less than half of 13 W (6.5 W).
steps: Series: emf = 10 V, internal resistance = 1.6 ohm; I = 10 / (4.0 + 1.6) = 1.79 A.
Series power P = I^2 R = 1.79^2 x 4.0 = 12.8 W, consistent with 13 W.
Parallel: emf = 5.0 V, internal resistance = 0.80 / 2 = 0.40 ohm.
Parallel current I = 5.0 / (4.0 + 0.40) = 1.14 A.
Parallel power P = 1.14^2 x 4.0 = 5.2 W.
Half of 13 W is 6.5 W; 5.2 W is less, so the student is correct.

questions.question: Which explains how electrons in a discharge tube produce an emission line spectrum? A: move to higher levels and absorb; B: move to higher levels and emit; C: move to lower levels and absorb; D: move to lower levels and emit.
questions.answer: D - excited electrons move to lower energy levels and emit photons.
steps: An emission line spectrum is produced when electrons fall to lower energy levels.
Each fall emits a photon with energy equal to the level difference.
Moving up (absorption) gives absorption lines, not emission lines.
So D is correct.

questions.question: In an atom, an electron drops from energy level E2 to energy level E1. A photon of wavelength lambda is emitted. Which expression gives the energy E2? A hc/lambda - E1; B hc/lambda + E1; C h lambda/c - E1; D h lambda/c + E1.
questions.answer: B: E2 = hc / lambda + E1.
steps: The photon energy equals the energy lost by the electron: hc / lambda = E2 - E1.
Rearranging gives E2 = hc / lambda + E1. The photon energy is hc/lambda (not h lambda/c), which rules out C and D.

questions.question: Which is evidence that electrons can behave like waves? A: attracted to positive charge; B: absorb photons between levels; C: diffracted through thin graphite; D: released by photons.
questions.answer: C - electrons can be diffracted when passing through a thin sheet of graphite.
steps: Diffraction is a wave property.
Electrons diffracted by thin graphite show wave behaviour.
A (attraction to charge) is an electrostatic effect, not a wave property.
B and D show particle-like energy exchange with photons, so C is the correct answer.

questions.question: Which describes threshold frequency? A: frequency giving maximum KE; B: frequency emitted by electrons falling to ground; C: minimum frequency to make an electron leave a surface; D: maximum frequency exciting a ground-state electron.
questions.answer: C - the minimum frequency of light that can cause an electron to leave a surface.
steps: Threshold frequency f0 = phi / h is the minimum frequency for photoemission.
Below f0 a photon lacks enough energy to free an electron.
Option A describes maximum KE, B describes line emission and D describes absorption.
Option C matches the definition.

questions.question: An electron has a de Broglie wavelength of 3.5 x 10^-10 m. Which expression gives the velocity of the electron in m s^-1? A 6.63 x 10^-34 / (9.11 x 10^-31 x 3.5 x 10^-10); B 6.63 x 10^-34 / 3.5 x 10^-10; C (9.11 x 10^-31 x 3.5 x 10^-10) / 6.63 x 10^-34; D 3.5 x 10^-10 / 6.63 x 10^-34.
steps: lambda = h / (m v), so v = h / (m lambda).
Option B leaves out the electron mass (it would give momentum, not velocity), and C and D are inverted. So A is correct.

questions.question: Light of wavelength lambda travelling at speed c is incident on a metal surface. Photoelectrons are emitted with a maximum kinetic energy (1/2)mv^2(max). The graph shows 1/lambda (y-axis) against (1/2)mv^2(max) (x-axis), a straight line. Which shows how the gradient can be used to determine the Planck constant h? A h = 1/gradient; B h = 1/(c x gradient); C h = c/gradient; D h = gradient.
questions.answer: B: h = 1 / (c x gradient).
steps: hf = phi + (1/2)mv^2, and f = c / lambda, so hc / lambda = phi + (1/2)mv^2.
Rearranging: 1/lambda = (1/hc) x (1/2)mv^2 + phi/(hc).
On a graph of 1/lambda against (1/2)mv^2, the gradient = 1/(hc), so h = 1 / (c x gradient).

questions.question: Which describes a change in energy of 1 eV? A: 1 C accelerated through 1 V; B: 1 C passes a point in 1 s; C: an electron accelerated through 1 V; D: 1 A for 1 s.
questions.answer: C - an electron accelerated through 1 V gains 1 eV.
steps: 1 eV = 1.60e-19 J = the energy gained by a charge e moved through 1 V (E = QV).
A: 1 C through 1 V gives 1 J, not 1 eV.
B and D describe charge flow (current), not energy change.
C: an electron (charge 1.60e-19 C) through 1 V gains 1 eV.

questions.question: Describe the photoelectric effect.
questions.answer: Electromagnetic radiation of frequency at or above threshold is absorbed by electrons in a metal surface, which are then emitted.
steps: A photon is absorbed by an electron at the metal surface.
If the photon energy hf is at least the work function, the electron is emitted.
Emission is effectively instantaneous.
The KE of emitted electrons depends on frequency, not intensity.

questions.question: Explain why a photomultiplier cannot detect some frequencies of electromagnetic radiation.
questions.answer: Photons below the threshold frequency have energy less than the work function, so no photoelectrons are emitted.
steps: Photoelectric emission requires hf at least equal to the work function.
Radiation below threshold frequency has photon energy below the work function.
Such photons cannot release electrons.
So the photomultiplier cannot detect these frequencies.

questions.question: Visible light spans 380 to 700 nm and the photocathode work function is 1.48 eV. Deduce whether the photomultiplier can detect all visible wavelengths.
questions.answer: Yes: threshold wavelength is about 840 nm, which is above 700 nm, so all visible light releases electrons.
steps: Work function in joules: 1.48 x 1.60e-19 = 2.37e-19 J.
Threshold wavelength lambda0 = hc / phi = (6.63e-34 x 3.00e8) / 2.37e-19 = 8.40e-7 m = 840 nm.
Photons with lambda below 840 nm have energy above the work function.
The longest visible wavelength is 700 nm, so its energy is 1.78 eV, above 1.48 eV.
Therefore all visible wavelengths (380 to 700 nm) are detected.

questions.question: An electron leaves the photocathode at 1.35e6 m/s and is accelerated through 108 V to the first plate. Calculate its kinetic energy in joules at the plate.
steps: Work done by the p.d. = eV = 1.60e-19 x 108 = 1.73e-17 J.
The electron gains this energy as it accelerates, so final KE = initial KE + work done.

questions.question: The circuit has four resistors A, B, C and D in series (each 85.0 kohm) connected across a power supply through a switch. When the switch is open, the p.d. across the power supply is 1960 V. When the switch is closed, the p.d. across resistor A is 108 V. Calculate the internal resistance of the power supply.
questions.answer: Internal resistance = 1.2 x 10^6 ohm (1.20 M ohm).
steps: The e.m.f. is the open-circuit p.d. = 1960 V.
The current in the series circuit I = V_A / R_A = 108 / 85 000 = 1.27 x 10^-3 A.
The p.d. across all four resistors (the terminal p.d.) = 4 x 108 = 432 V, so the lost volts = 1960 - 432 = 1528 V.

questions.question: Particle X of mass m is moving with velocity v and has a de Broglie wavelength lambda. Particle Y has a de Broglie wavelength 0.25 lambda. Which row could give the mass and velocity of particle Y? A 0.25m, v; B 0.5m, 8v; C m, 2v; D 2m, 4v.
questions.answer: B: mass 0.5m and velocity 8v.
steps: lambda = h / (m v), so a wavelength 0.25 times as big needs a momentum 4 times as big: m_Y v_Y = 4 m v.
B: 0.5m x 8v = 4 m v, which works.
A gives 0.25 mv, C gives 2 mv and D gives 8 mv, none of which equal 4 mv.

questions.question: A student stands a distance d from a wall. She makes a loud sound and hears the echo of the sound from the wall after a time t. Which expression gives the speed of the sound wave? A 2d/t; B d/t; C d/(2t); D 2t/d.
questions.answer: A: v = 2d / t.
steps: The sound travels to the wall and back, a total distance of 2d, in time t.
speed = distance / time = 2d / t.

questions.question: Explain why a beam of monochromatic light, with all photons of equal energy, produces photoelectrons with a range of kinetic energies.
questions.answer: Electrons lose different amounts of energy in the metal before escaping, so KE ranges from zero up to the maximum.
steps: All photons have the same energy hf.
Electrons are released from different depths inside the metal.
Electrons from deeper inside lose energy in collisions before reaching the surface.
Electrons escaping from the surface keep the maximum KE = hf - phi.
So KE values range from zero up to the maximum.

questions.question: Explain what the observations (white light at low or high intensity gives no current; low-intensity UV gives a current) show about the nature of light.
questions.answer: Light acts as photons: emission depends on photon frequency (above threshold), not on intensity.
steps: White light at high intensity gave no current, so its photon frequencies are below the threshold.
Intensity alone cannot release electrons when each photon is below threshold.
Low-intensity UV gave a current, so its photons have frequency above threshold.
Even a few photons above threshold eject electrons, so the energy of each photon matters.
This supports a particle (photon) model of light, with energy E = hf.

questions.question: The scientist reversed the connections to the 1.5 V battery so that the electrode is at a lower potential than the plate (negligible internal resistance). When photoelectrons have enough kinetic energy to overcome the potential difference across the photocell, there is a current. Ultraviolet light of wavelength 250 nm is incident on the photocell. Work function of the metal plate = 6.9 x 10^-19 J. Deduce whether there is a current in the circuit.
questions.answer: No current: the maximum kinetic energy (1.06 x 10^-19 J, 0.66 eV) is less than the 1.5 eV needed to overcome the 1.5 V p.d.
steps: Maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons = 7.96 x 10^-19 - 6.9 x 10^-19 = 1.06 x 10^-19 J (0.66 eV).
With the battery reversed, the electrons are repelled by the electrode. To reach it each needs kinetic energy of at least eV = 1.60 x 10^-19 x 1.5 = 2.40 x 10^-19 J.
1.06 x 10^-19 J is less than 2.40 x 10^-19 J (equivalent to a stopping p.d. of 0.66 V against 1.5 V), so no electrons cross the gap and there is no current.

questions.question: A car sensor emits a sound pulse and detects the echo after time t, with speed of sound v. Which gives the distance to the object? A: 2vt; B: 2vt-1; C: 0.5vt; D: 0.5vt-1.
steps: The pulse travels to the object and back, so total distance = v t.
Distance to the object is half the total: v t / 2 = 0.5 vt.
Options A and B give double the distance; B and D include an extra -1 term with no physical meaning.
So C is correct.

questions.question: The diagram shows the energy needed for an electron in the ground state of a mercury atom to move to different energy levels: 4.91 eV, 5.46 eV, 6.70 eV and 7.73 eV above the ground state. Photons transfer 8.74 x 10^-19 J to electrons in the ground state of mercury atoms. Which gives the number of different frequencies of light that could be emitted? A 1; B 3; C 6; D 10.
questions.answer: B: 3 different frequencies.
steps: The energy transferred in eV = 8.74 x 10^-19 / 1.60 x 10^-19 = 5.46 eV, so electrons are excited to the 5.46 eV level only.
From the 5.46 eV level an electron can fall to 4.91 eV, or to the ground state; an electron at 4.91 eV can then fall to the ground state.
The possible transitions are 5.46 to 4.91, 5.46 to 0 and 4.91 to 0: three different photon energies, so three frequencies.

questions.question: An electron moves with velocity 3.6e7 m/s. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength.
steps: de Broglie wavelength lambda = h / (m v).
The speed is about 0.12c, so the non-relativistic formula is valid.

questions.question: Determine whether the transducer can detect ultrasound reflected from a crack 4.0 cm away in concrete at 23 C, pulse duration 200 us (speed-temperature graph missing).
questions.answer: No: the echo returns after about 19 microseconds while the 200 microsecond pulse is still being emitted, so the pulses overlap and the crack cannot be detected.
steps: The graph is a straight line from 4000 m s^-1 at 0 deg C to 4200 m s^-1 at 40 deg C, a gradient of 5 m s^-1 per deg C, so at 23 deg C v = 4000 + 5 x 23 = 4115 m s^-1.
The pulse travels to the crack and back: distance = 2 x 4.0 cm = 0.080 m.
Time for the echo = 0.080 / 4115 = 1.9 x 10^-5 s = 19 microseconds.
The pulse lasts 200 microseconds, so the reflected pulse arrives back while the transducer is still sending: the pulses overlap and the reflection cannot be detected.

questions.question: Explain why pulses of ultrasound with a higher frequency are used to find cracks of shorter length.
questions.answer: Higher frequency means shorter wavelength (lambda = v/f), and a shorter wavelength can detect smaller cracks.
steps: Wavelength lambda = v / f, so higher frequency gives shorter wavelength.
A wave can only detect features comparable to or larger than its wavelength.
A shorter wavelength therefore resolves smaller cracks.
Hence the higher frequency is used for shorter cracks.

questions.question: State what is meant by diffraction.
questions.answer: Diffraction is the spreading of waves when they pass through a gap or round an obstacle, most noticeable when the gap is comparable to the wavelength.
steps: Diffraction is the spreading of a wave as it passes through a gap or around an edge.
The spreading is greatest when the gap size is comparable to the wavelength.
Electron diffraction through graphite is an example, producing a pattern on the screen.
This shows electrons behave as waves.

questions.question: An electron is accelerated through 4.9 kV. Show that its de Broglie wavelength is about 1.8e-11 m.
questions.answer: lambda = 1.75e-11 m, i.e. about 1.8e-11 m (shown).
steps: Kinetic energy gained: KE = eV = 1.60e-19 x 4900 = 7.84e-16 J.
Momentum p = sqrt(2 m KE) = sqrt(2 x 9.11e-31 x 7.84e-16) = 3.78e-23 kg m s-1.
de Broglie wavelength lambda = h / p = 6.63e-34 / 3.78e-23.
lambda = 1.75e-11 m, about 1.8e-11 m.

questions.question: Deduce whether a second order maximum would be clearly visible for electrons (lambda 1.8e-11 m) through a 5000 lines/cm grating with screen about 1 m away.
questions.answer: No: the second-order maximum is only about 18 micrometres from the centre, too close to be clearly seen.
steps: Line spacing d = 1 / (5000 per cm) = 1 / (5.0e5 per m) = 2.0e-6 m.
Second order: sin(theta) = 2 lambda / d = 2 x 1.8e-11 / 2.0e-6 = 1.8e-5.
Position on screen x = D tan(theta) = 1.0 x 1.8e-5 = 1.8e-5 m.
This is only about 18 micrometres from the central maximum, too small to be seen clearly.

questions.question: Explain why the mercury atoms in the UV lamp emit photons after electrons collide with them.
questions.answer: Collisions excite mercury electrons to higher levels; when they fall back, photons are emitted.
steps: Electrons from the high p.d. collide with mercury atoms and transfer energy.
Mercury electrons are excited to higher energy levels.
The excited electrons fall back to lower levels.
Each fall emits a photon with energy equal to the level difference.

questions.question: A technician replaces the screen on a mobile phone. The equipment and screen dimensions (7.15 cm wide, 14.7 cm long) are shown. The intensity of the UV light received on the screen is 50 mW cm^-2. The glue takes 25 s to harden. Show that the total energy incident on the glass screen during this time is about 130 J.
questions.answer: E = 131 J, which is about 130 J.
steps: Area of the screen = 7.15 cm x 14.7 cm = 105 cm^2.
Power received = intensity x area = 50 mW cm^-2 x 105 cm^2 = 5260 mW = 5.26 W.
Energy = power x time = 5.26 W x 25 s = 131 J, about 130 J.

questions.question: Using the 130 J total energy with UV wavelength 395 nm, determine the number of photons incident on the glass screen.
questions.answer: About 2.6e20 photons
steps: Energy per photon E = hc / lambda.
Use the total energy of 130 J from part (i).

questions.question: Explain the effect on the frequency of UV produced when the p.d. across the lamp electrodes is increased.
questions.answer: A higher p.d. gives electrons more kinetic energy, so collisions can excite atoms to higher levels, producing higher-frequency photons.
steps: KE of electrons from the p.d.: KE = eV, so a higher V gives higher KE.
More energetic electrons can excite atoms to higher energy levels.
Transitions between higher levels release photons of greater energy.
Greater photon energy means higher frequency UV is produced.

questions.question: Suggest why the glue hardens faster when the UV lamp is moved closer to the phone screen.
questions.answer: Moving closer raises the intensity received (inverse square law), so the same total energy is delivered in less time.
steps: Intensity from a point source is I = P / (4 pi r^2), so it rises as r falls.
A higher intensity delivers more UV energy per second to the glue.
The total energy required is fixed at about 130 J.
So the hardening time is reduced.

questions.question: When monochromatic light is incident on the surface of a metal, photoelectrons are emitted. Which statement is correct? A The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons depends on the intensity of the incident light. B The number of photoelectrons emitted per second depends on the frequency of the incident light. C The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons depends on the frequency of the incident light. D The number of photoelectrons emitted per second depends on the work function of the metal.
questions.answer: C: the maximum kinetic energy depends on the frequency of the incident light.
steps: Each photon gives all its energy hf to one electron, so E_k(max) = hf - phi depends on the frequency (and the work function), which makes C correct.

Intensity only changes the number of photons per second, so A is wrong, and the number of electrons per second depends on the intensity (not on the frequency or the work function), so B and D are wrong.

questions.question: Which transition (arrows A to D on the hydrogen energy level diagram) would emit a photon with the shortest wavelength?
questions.answer: A.
steps: A photon is emitted when an electron falls to a lower level, so only A and D (downward arrows) are emissions; B and C are upward (absorption).
Photon wavelength lambda = hc / Delta E, so the shortest wavelength comes from the largest energy drop.
A is a drop of 13.6 eV (0 to -13.6) but D is only 3.39 eV (0 to -3.39), so A emits the photon with the shortest wavelength.
